nodes.content: Enable zero-shot voice conversion across unseen tonal languages while transferring speaker identity without altering lexical tone or prosody.
requirements: Keep lexical-tone error within 2 percentage points of unconverted speech, preserving source intonation and rhythm.
Achieve 90% target-speaker verification acceptance at 1% false acceptance using evaluators independent of training.

nodes.content: Condition a zero-shot flow vocoder on XLS-R content, source F0, energy, and durations, plus pitch-adversarial target-speaker embeddings.
Can pitch-adversarial target embeddings transfer identity without target-reference F0 overwriting source lexical tones?
Pitch-adversarial embeddings yield ≤2-point ToneER increase and ≥90% independent target-speaker acceptance at 1% FAR on unseen tonal languages.
Train pitch-adversarial and baseline vocoders; test held-out Thai and Yoruba with ToneER, F0/rhythm errors, and independent speaker verification.
Benchmark adversarial versus baseline embeddings on 500 held-out Thai/Yoruba utterances: ToneER, F0, timing, and independent 1%-FAR speaker acceptance.
On held-out Thai/Yoruba, unconverted/adversarial/baseline ToneER was 4.8%/6.2%/8.1%; adversarial embeddings achieved 91% independent-speaker acceptance at 1% FAR.
Select pitch-adversarial embeddings for further prosody validation: ToneER increased 1.4 points and independent speaker acceptance reached 91%.
Validate selected adversarial embeddings on held-out Thai/Yoruba: source F0-contour correlation ≥0.95 and syllable-duration MAE ≤25 ms.
Align the 500 held-out Thai/Yoruba source–conversion pairs; measure voiced F0-contour correlation and syllable-duration MAE against source prosody.
Thai/Yoruba prosody audit with source–conversion alignments, per-utterance voiced F0 correlation, syllable-duration MAE, and audio links.
Inspect 100 stratified audit alignments against audio, recalculating F0 correlation and syllable-duration MAE to detect alignment errors.
Audio-validated Thai/Yoruba alignments (98/100) showed voiced F0 correlation of 0.96 and syllable-duration MAE of 19 ms.
For source–target median-F0 gaps ≥6 semitones, residual embedding leakage raises Thai/Yoruba ToneER over 2 points above unconverted speech.
Stratify 500 Thai/Yoruba pairs by source–target median-F0 gap; compare ToneER increases above and below 6 semitones.
At ≥6-semitone gaps, Thai/Yoruba ToneER rose from 5.0% unconverted to 6.6% converted, below the hypothesized 2-point increase.
Does independent 1%-FAR target-speaker acceptance remain ≥90% for source–target F0 gaps ≥6 semitones?
Recompute independent 1%-FAR speaker acceptance on ≥6-semitone-gap Thai/Yoruba pairs, with bootstrap confidence intervals and a <6-semitone comparison.
F0-gap speaker-verification report with fixed independent 1%-FAR threshold, stratified acceptance rates, bootstrap intervals, and pair counts.
Use target-conditioned spectral-envelope diffusion with source harmonic excitation, retaining original F0 trajectories and timing for unseen-language conversion.
Can target-conditioned spectral-envelope diffusion achieve ≥90% independent speaker acceptance at 1% FAR while retaining source harmonic excitation?
Target-conditioned envelope diffusion reaches ≥90% independent 1%-FAR speaker acceptance without source F0 or duration modification on held-out Thai/Yoruba.
Using n17’s fixed 1%-FAR threshold, benchmark envelope diffusion on held-out Thai/Yoruba for speaker acceptance, F0 correlation, and duration MAE.
Envelope diffusion yielded 84% independent 1%-FAR speaker acceptance; source-F0 correlation was 0.98 and syllable-duration MAE 12 ms.
Adding target-conditioned glottal spectral tilt to envelope diffusion raises independent 1%-FAR acceptance to ≥90% without changing source F0.
Ablate target-conditioned glottal tilt on held-out Thai/Yoruba; compare fixed-threshold speaker acceptance, ToneER, and source-F0 correlation against envelope diffusion.
Glottal-tilt diffusion raised independent 1%-FAR acceptance from 84% to 92%; source-F0 correlation was 0.98 and ToneER rose 1.3 points.
Select glottal-tilt diffusion: 92% speaker acceptance, 0.98 F0 correlation, and 1.3-point ToneER increase outperform adversarial conversion.
Test selected glottal-tilt diffusion on unseen Cantonese/Vietnamese for ≤2-point ToneER increase, F0/rhythm fidelity, and ≥90% independent 1%-FAR speaker acceptance.
Convert 500 held-out Cantonese/Vietnamese utterances; score ToneER, F0 correlation, syllable-duration MAE, and independent 1%-FAR speaker acceptance.
Cantonese/Vietnamese transfer report with paired audio, baseline/converted ToneER, F0 correlation, duration MAE, and independent 1%-FAR speaker acceptance.
Independently re-audit Thai/Yoruba prosody alignments and Cantonese/Vietnamese transfer scores against paired audio, recalculating each report’s metrics.
Full-cohort audit: adversarial Thai/Yoruba F0 correlation was 0.91 (<0.95); diffusion Cantonese/Vietnamese ToneER rose 1.5 points, with 92% independent 1%-FAR acceptance.
After the audit, benchmark both converters on matched Cantonese/Vietnamese pairs for ToneER, F0 correlation, duration MAE, and independent 1%-FAR acceptance.
Matched Cantonese/Vietnamese: diffusion/adversarial ToneER increases were 1.5/2.4 points, F0 correlations 0.98/0.90, duration MAE 13/24 ms, independent 1%-FAR acceptance 92%/88%.
Does target-conditioned envelope diffusion preserve Cantonese/Vietnamese vowel contrasts while transferring target timbre, as measured by independent phoneme error?
Using n32’s matched cohort, audit n28’s report for omitted vowel substitutions; compare both converters’ independently scored phoneme-error rates.
Vowel-aware audit found 9% Cantonese/Vietnamese vowel substitutions; corrected diffusion ToneER rose 2.6 points, versus previously reported 1.5.
Suspend both converters pending vowel-preserving redesign: corrected diffusion ToneER rises 2.6 points; adversarial fails tone, F0, and speaker thresholds.
Constrain glottal-tilt diffusion with source vowel-formant anchors and phoneme-consistency loss, retaining source F0 and syllable timing.
Can source vowel-formant anchors reduce corrected ToneER below 2 points without lowering independent speaker acceptance below 90%?
Source-formant anchors plus phoneme consistency reduce corrected ToneER increase to ≤1.8 points while retaining ≥90% independent 1%-FAR speaker acceptance.
Following suspension, train formant-anchored, phoneme-consistent diffusion; ablate each constraint on held-out Cantonese/Vietnamese using corrected ToneER and independent speaker verification.
Train four glottal-tilt variants crossing formant anchors and phoneme-consistency loss; score Cantonese/Vietnamese with n17’s fixed independent 1%-FAR threshold.
Four-variant Cantonese/Vietnamese ablation table with corrected ToneER increases, vowel-substitution rates, and fixed-threshold independent speaker acceptance.
Reaudit n41’s vowel substitutions against n35’s corrected baseline; recompute ToneER increases and independent 1%-FAR speaker acceptance.
Reaudit: dual constraints reduced vowel substitutions 9%→3%, corrected ToneER increase to 1.7 points; independent 1%-FAR speaker acceptance reached 91%.
For source–target vowel F2 gaps ≥300 Hz, do formant anchors maintain ≥90% independent 1%-FAR speaker acceptance?
Following suspension, stratify n41’s n43-audited dual-constraint conversions by ≥300-Hz versus <300-Hz F2 gaps; compare independent 1%-FAR acceptance and corrected ToneER.
For ≥300-Hz F2 gaps, dual-constraint diffusion achieved 90% independent 1%-FAR speaker acceptance and a 1.8-point corrected ToneER increase.
Conditionally reinstate diffusion: overall 1.7-point/91%, high-F2 1.8-point/90%; require full-cohort prosody audit against n11’s audio-validated F0/timing benchmarks.
